html:
The silver and gold roll was the pay system the United States used in the Panama Canal Zone, which split workers by race and origin. Skilled workers, almost all white Americans, were on the "gold roll" and paid in US gold coin, with better housing, food and leave. Everyone else was on the "silver roll", paid in the weaker silver currency of Panama.

Most of the silver workers came from the Caribbean, above all Barbados, with others from Jamaica, Martinique and southern Europe. They built much of the Panama Canal by hand. They lived in worse housing and ate in separate commissaries, and the Zone had segregated schools, post offices and clubs in the manner of the American South. Many died of accident and disease.

The system began as the building of the canal got under way in 1905 under chief engineer John Stevens and then George Goethals. The terms "gold" and "silver" were officially dropped in 1948, but unequal pay and segregation lasted for years in the Zone. The descendants of silver roll workers became a large part of Panama's population, and their long fight for rights is a lasting result of the canal.
